So my favorite science fiction author. A grandmaster of the genre, Frederick Pohl passed away a year or so ago.

I recently had the pleasure of finding his final novel, the titled story, in a library. The book came out in 2011 when Pohl was 93or so. I've passively wondered for a few years what God opinion on LGBT people was, and I think this book answered it fairly well.

The gay characters are actual, nuanced characters, and their sexuality was a minor part of most of their identities, which I though was awesome. Have me a resounding "I really don't give a fuck what people smash their genitals into" vibe.

The reason I'm posting this here is because there is a... Transgender(wish) character relevant to the plot. I want to know what v/transpeople thinks of this character, and the authors handling of them.

I'd say more, but it would contain spoilers, and threw me for a loop. I'll wait until someone here has read the book before giving my spoiler heavy opinions about it.

If no one cares to read the book, but wants to hear about it, let me know and I'll post anyway.

With love,

Drostan.
"All The Lives He Led" by Frederick Pohl

So, All the Lives He Led takes place in 2076, in the aftermath of the eruption of Yellowstone, which basically wiped the US off the map. The world economy has gone crazy, and many US refugees sign up for indentured servitude to reach for a better life.

The main character, Brad, works at Pompeii, now a theme park, on the eve of the 2000 year anniversary of Vesuvius's eruption. It's here he meets Gerda Fleming, and falls in love with her.

Several chapters of plot later, it's revealed that she has something to do with a terrorist attack, which is spreading a deadly virus around the world. International Security (referred to just as Security) reveals to Brad that his lovely Gerda was in fact a world renown terrorist, named (I forgot his name, but male).

Security tries to use that information to force Brad to give up her whereabouts, something he doesn't know to begin with. He is a bit surprised that his girl used to be a boy, and feels a little betrayed, but loves her anyway.

When Security finds Gerda's location, they take Brad as bait, and when they ultimately kill her, Brad is there to hold her as she dies.

 

Now Gerda isn't necessarily the good guy, but not because of her gender identity, and the main character still loves her deeply, even recreating get research and keeping a new world ending disease close (just in case).

Now the reason I said trans(ish) before was because Gerda had a gender change to hide her identity, but the book details the characters transition quite graphically. Being a terrorist, who was presumed dead, and gravely injured, she had to go to a criminal organization in order to perform the process, which is painfully detailed. After the transition, the character adapts and apparently seems preferential to her gender.

She's not a perfect trans character by a long shot, but I think coming from the brain of a 93 year old, straight cis male, Gerda is a great, if completely unorthodox, exploration of a characters gender identity.

Nowhere in the book are gay or transgender characters bashed, except when Security tries to get under Brad's skin, and Brad passing over male suiters.

That's another thing. Brad only once called Gerda a "he/she... Gerda..." When he has just found out.

 

The book isn't Pohls best with e from a literary standpoint, but it fucking warmed my heart and almost made me cry.

Title says it all. Microsoft says above 4 for C# but what are your opinions / experience when it comes to depth of inherience?

https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/ms182213.aspx
When does inherience trees in your opinions get too deep? (C#/C++)

Around 3-4 sounds about right for an application, anything beyond that could probably be refactored. The exception to that would be if you're designing a framework, where it could be very useful to break that rule to provide a cleaner API.

This. There are some problems with object-oriented as a paradigm, and composition is an interesting alternative that has a lot of benefits if your type system can back it up. No individual paradigm makes 'the right' compromises in every situation--even as I'm driving toward protocol-based composition as my primary tool in Swift, I still am very glad to have good ol' classes around for a handful of situations.

I think that you should consider that, anywhere you have an inheritance tree deeper than three or four, you should ask yourself if you're encapsulating your variation correctly. Ideally, if you have fourth and fifth derivative objects, then they should spend most of their lives being treated as anonymous concrete instances of some superclass at the third or fourth level.

Deep inheritance usually means you are inheriting along multiple "axes" of variability. In a language without interfaces or multiple inheritance (and sometimes even in those) you should model multi-dimensional objects with composition.

There are exceptions of course, especially if you are making an extensible framework.
